title: An experimental method to investigate the water-based suppression of smoldering peat fire
author: Lin, Huang
materials: Unlike the visible flaming fire, it is difficult to judge the effectiveness and success of suppressing the smoldering fire, especially in the deep soil layer. Therefore, an array of armored K-type thermocouples with 1-mm bead diameter were inserted into the peat sample at different depths to monitor the temperature and the location of the smoldering front [9,10]. In general, the interval between the thermocouples should not be lower than 2 cm and be larger than 5 cm. After ignition, the basket of peat sample was placed into a larger cylindrical mesh basket with a diameter of > 2D and a height of h. In order to simulate the natural state and mimic a real boundary condition, the space between two baskets was filled with unheated peat soils [1]. Note that the coil igniter will not be removed after the ignition so as not to damage the upper structure of the sample. Afterward, the entire setup was left to burn and self-stabilize for another 30 min before the start of water suppression.

For smoldering peat fire, the cylindrical reactor we used had a diameter of 10 cm and a height of 15 cm. And four thermocouples were inserted into the peat sample at different depths at 0 cm (surface), 5 cm, 10 cm and 15 cm to monitor the temperature. The coil heater was buried 5 cm below the top free surface, and the ignition protocol was 60 W for 60 min. Fig. 4a shows a group of thermocouple measurements of the baseline experiment without suppression, and a typical smoldering spread over a 15-cm deep peat sample can last for about 350 min (about 6 h).Fig. 4Temperature measurement of (a) base case without rain suppression, and (b) successful suppression with rainfall intensity of 35 mm/h for 40 min.Fig 4

steps.title: Collect and preprocess peat soil
steps.instruction: Obtain peat soil from field or market; commercial peat is preferred for uniform density, particle size and organic content. Dry the peat in an oven at a constant 40 °C, monitoring weight and moisture every 1 h until the moisture content reaches the target value (e.g., 50 %). Avoid higher temperatures to prevent hydrophobicity changes. After drying, shake the sample, seal it in a box and let it homogenize for at least 48 h. Check the moisture content again before the experiment.

steps.title: Prepare cylindrical mesh reactor
steps.instruction: Use a steel‑mesh cylindrical basket with diameter D > 10 cm and height h > 15 cm (height‑to‑diameter ratio ≥ 1:1). Fill the basket with the peat sample and compress it slightly to obtain a dry bulk density of about 145 kg m⁻³ regardless of moisture content. Place this basket inside a larger cylindrical mesh basket whose diameter is > 2 D and height h; fill the annular space with unheated peat soil to mimic natural boundary conditions.

steps.title: Insert thermocouples
steps.instruction: Insert armored K‑type thermocouples (1‑mm bead diameter) into the peat at depths of 0 cm (surface), 5 cm, 10 cm and 15 cm (or at any spacing between 2 cm and 5 cm). Ensure the thermocouples are securely positioned to monitor temperature and smoldering front location.

steps.title: Place coil igniter
steps.instruction: Insert a long Cr20Ni80 coil igniter at the desired depth below the top free surface (e.g., 5 cm) to allow study of both shallow and deep smoldering fire spread. The igniter will remain in place throughout the experiment.

steps.title: Ignite peat sample
steps.instruction: Activate the coil igniter with either 60 W for 60 min or 100 W for 30 min, depending on peat condition, to initiate a robust smoldering fire.

steps.title: Allow self‑stabilization
steps.instruction: Turn off the power supply after the ignition period and let the peat burn for an additional 30 min to self‑stabilize and confirm successful ignition before any water‑based suppression is applied.

steps.title: Configure wet chamber and sprinkler
steps.instruction: Set up the wet chamber (30 m²) with ambient temperature 23 °C, relative humidity 50 % and pressure 1 atm. Install a sprinkler system consisting of a nozzle, pressure gauge and valve; position the nozzle at a height > 2 m above the sample. Adjust the nozzle‑to‑sample distance as needed. Set water pressure P (e.g., 500 kPa) and use a nozzle orifice diameter D of 15 mm. The surface tension of the air‑water interface is σ = 0.073 N m⁻¹. A fan may be installed but is not used in this protocol.

steps.title: Measure water‑spray intensity (optional)
steps.instruction: Place cylindrical containers (same diameter and height as the reactor) at various locations. Run the sprinkler for a fixed duration Δt = 15 min, measure the water height d in each container, and calculate local intensity I = d/Δt (mm h⁻¹). Position the peat sample at a location that provides the desired intensity. Time‑dependent intensities can be simulated by varying water pressure P over time or moving the sample (position R).

steps.title: Apply water‑based suppression
steps.instruction: Move the prepared peat reactor to the prescribed location inside the chamber. Activate the sprinkler for the prescribed duration (e.g., 40 min at an intensity of 35 mm h⁻¹). After the spray period, shut off the sprinkler.

steps.title: Post‑suppression monitoring
steps.instruction: Leave the sample undisturbed for 24 h while continuously recording thermocouple temperatures. If any temperature rises above 250 °C (the minimum smoldering temperature of peat) or the peat eventually burns out, classify the suppression as a failure and repeat the test to confirm the outcome.

steps.title: Iterate to find critical conditions
steps.instruction: Using fresh peat samples, repeat steps 5‑10 while varying water‑spray duration, intensity and igniter depth until the combination of water‑spray duration and depth that reliably suppresses the smoldering fire is identified.

steps.title: Conduct flaming wood‑crib reference test
steps.instruction: Construct a wood crib from cylindrical wood rods 8 cm long and 1 cm diameter, giving an area comparable to the peat reactor. Ignite the crib with a lighter for 1 min, allow 1 min of self‑burning, then activate the same sprinkler system (e.g., 500 kPa, 15 mm nozzle) for about 40 s. Judge extinction visually; the test follows the same evaluation criteria as the smoldering experiments.

steps.title: Calculate median droplet size (optional)
steps.instruction: Use the empirical correlation dm = C·D^{2/3}·σ^{1/3}·P^{1/3} with σ = 0.073 N m⁻¹, D = 15 mm and P ≈ 500 kPa to estimate the median water droplet diameter (dm ≈ 1 mm). Adjust C according to the specific nozzle if needed.
